field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1239) — Under the Flora name Andropogon glomeratus, look for many short flowering branches crowded into a broom-shaped cluster. The Flora gives branch lengths of 1.5–3 cm.

Bushy bluestem is a tufted perennial with erect culms often about 75–150 cm in Kew GrassBase. Numerous crowded short flowering units make a broad, cottony terminal brush, unlike broomsedge's more separated spathe-held units. Texas Uvalde whole-clump and USGS flowering photographs show this gross architecture; a white head alone is not definitive.

True ligule: although the ligule is a 1–2 mm papery membrane, its margin is ciliate and can carry long fine hairs. Choose a visible hair fringe only when the hairs arise from the actual inner membrane; never confuse the long hairs on sheath margins, nearby spathes or flowering spikelets with a hair-only ligule. The broomlike flowering arrangement and paired florets remain more diagnostic.

A compact mature CANE BLUESTEM panicle can make a fan of several near-terminal ascending racemes; under the broad filter a finger-like silhouette is therefore compatible. field_rule:
TALL GRAMA B. pectinata is usually robust with 3–5 often relatively long straight combs; B. hirsuta has pronounced branch hairs and bare 'stinger' but can overlap in branch count and rachis tip. Blue grama mostly 1–3 curved eyebrows, spikelets tending to extend to branch tip; Texas grama very short woolly/awned groups; red grama thin wiry small appressed racemes. Avoid a species diagnosis from size or branch count alone.

Ligule and awn caution: FNA treats this as B. hirsuta subsp. pectinata, and its parent B. hirsuta description reports a tiny hair ligule; that supports the current hair choice. Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015) describes a ciliate membrane for B. hirsuta, but did NOT separately treat B. pectinata, and the present tall-grama gallery does not show its true inner ligule. Do not assume a photographed outer collar hair proves a membrane; keep the membrane alternative pending taxon-specific or same-specimen evidence. FNA's B. hirsuta complex has short floret awns, but no tall-grama fertile/sterile floret is resolved in these photos. 'None obvious' means no conspicuous long awns at whole-head scale, NOT truly awnless. Do not select Aristida-style three long awns from a grama comb.

Scoring audit 2026-11-13: Tall grama's long pectinate combs also align their spikelets on one side. This broad match is valid but not an ID; verify mature spikelets and beware hairy-grama intermediates.

field_rule:
B. rigidiseta typically has several (often about 5–9) SHORT bristly/awned units near the top. Blue grama has only about 1–3 long curved combs. Sideoats grama carries many short pendant oats down a much longer axis. Red grama has narrower, more appressed, often purplish branches and awned spikelets; color alone is not sufficient. If an entire culm/branch cannot be resolved, keep Bouteloua sp.

Rootstock and collar caveat: the Hill Country description calls Texas grama a tufted non-rhizomatous perennial with a hair-fringe ligule, and Flora of North America agrees on the missing rhizomes but instead describes a tiny ciliate membrane. The UT Austin Williamson County account documents very short, shallow rhizomes and a membranous-ciliate ligule. A verified node-bearing underground stem or a visible membranous ligule base should therefore keep this candidate in the key, but neither observation alone confirms its identification. The present gallery lacks a rootstock or ligule view.

field_rule:
WOODED PERENNIAL BROME: confirm durable crown and true hairs on mature lemmas; match a measured spikelet and sheath/collar photo before separating native pubescens from annual bromes.

True ligule: Hairy woodland brome typically shows an erose membranous ligule. The Hill Country flora reports that its membrane margin can occasionally carry sparse cilia; an observer who sees those fine hairs at the true inner junction can still select a hair fringe without excluding it. Verify the perennial crown and hairy mature lemmas.

Scoring check: awns on this species are often only 3–8 mm, so the field answer 'no conspicuous LONG awns' can be appropriate even though the lemmas truly bear short awns. Both visual options are supported as coarse routes; inspect an intact spikelet with a hand lens before concluding awnless.
